<!-- Generated by go run ./internal/conn3x/provider/moddoc in conn3xorg/conn3x. Don't edit by hand. -->

One iptables or ip6tables rule in one chain, checked with iptables -C, added with -A or -I and deleted with -D. The rest of the chain is left alone.

Use `iptables_rule` on a host that runs neither firewalld nor ufw and keeps its firewall in plain iptables. Each step is one rule in one chain, and the rest of the chain is left alone, so it sits happily beside rules Docker, Kubernetes or an old script put there. To own a whole table instead, use [`nftables`](/modules/nftables).

## Example usage

Let SSH in, then replies to connections the host made:

```hcl
step "ssh" {
  iptables_rule {
    chain            = "INPUT"
    protocol         = "tcp"
    destination_port = "22"
    jump             = "ACCEPT"
    comment          = "ssh, managed by Conn3x"
    confirm_after    = "60s"
  }
}

step "replies" {
  iptables_rule {
    chain    = "INPUT"
    ctstate  = ["ESTABLISHED", "RELATED"]
    jump     = "ACCEPT"
    position = "insert"
  }
}
```

Open the web ports to one network, over IPv4 and IPv6, and keep both across reboots on Debian or Ubuntu:

```hcl
step "persistent" {
  package {
    name = "iptables-persistent"
  }
}

step "web" {
  for_each   = { ipv4 = "10.0.0.0/8", ipv6 = "fd00::/8" }
  depends_on = [conn3x_package.docs__persistent]

  iptables_rule {
    ip_version        = item.key
    chain             = "INPUT"
    protocol          = "tcp"
    source            = item.value
    destination_ports = ["80", "443"]
    jump              = "ACCEPT"
    persist           = true
  }
}
```

The address is the step's resource address, `conn3x_package.CIRCUIT__STEP`, here in a circuit named `docs`.

## Arguments

| Name | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `chain` | string | Yes | The chain, such as INPUT, FORWARD or a chain of your own. It must already exist. |
| `comment` | string | No | A comment kept with the rule, as -m comment --comment, so iptables -L shows who added it. It's part of the rule. |
| `confirm_after` | string | No | For a rule change that could lock Conn3x out, such as removing the rule that lets SSH in, or a ufw deny on its port: before the change, the host schedules its own undo after this long, such as "60s"; after it, Conn3x logs in again over a new connection and cancels it. If that login doesn't come, the host takes the change back by itself, even if Conn3x has gone away. Needs systemd. |
| `ctstate` | list of string | No | Connection states, such as ["ESTABLISHED", "RELATED"], as -m conntrack --ctstate. |
| `destination` | string | No | An address or CIDR network the packet goes to, as -d. |
| `destination_port` | string | One of | A port, such as 22, or a range, such as 6000:6007, as --dport. Set this or destination_ports. |
| `destination_ports` | list of string | One of | Up to 15 ports or ranges, as -m multiport --dports. Set this or destination_port. |
| `in_interface` | string | No | The interface the packet comes in on, as -i. A trailing + matches a prefix, such as eth+. |
| `ip_version` | string | No | "ipv4" (default) uses iptables, "ipv6" uses ip6tables. For both, use two steps. |
| `jump` | string | No | The target, such as ACCEPT, DROP, REJECT or a chain of your own, as -j. Unset, the rule only counts packets. |
| `on_remove` | string | No | "delete" (default) deletes the rule when the step is removed or replaced, "forget" leaves it. |
| `out_interface` | string | No | The interface the packet goes out on, as -o. |
| `persist` | bool | No | Save the whole table after every change, so it comes back at boot: iptables-save to /etc/iptables/rules.v4 (rules.v6) for iptables-persistent on Debian and Ubuntu, or /etc/sysconfig/iptables (ip6tables) for iptables-services on the Red Hat family. Fails when neither is installed. |
| `position` | string | No | "append" (default) adds the rule at the end of the chain, "insert" at the top, or at rule_num. Only used when the rule is added: a rule that's there anywhere in the chain counts. |
| `protocol` | string | No | tcp, udp, icmp, all or another protocol iptables knows, as -p. Ports need tcp, udp, udplite, sctp or dccp. |
| `rule_num` | number | No | With position = "insert", where the rule goes, from 1 at the top. |
| `source` | string | No | An address or CIDR network the packet comes from, as -s. |
| `source_port` | string | No | A port, such as 53, or a range, such as 1024:65535, as --sport. |
| `table` | string | No | filter (default), nat, mangle, raw or security. |

## Read-only attributes

Conn3x sets these; reference them as `conn3x_iptables_rule.<circuit>__<step>["<host>"].<name>`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `in_sync` | bool | Whether iptables -C found the rule at the last refresh. |
| `revision` | string | Changes each time Conn3x changes this on the host. Handlers watch it. |

A step lowers to the `conn3x_iptables_rule` resource, one instance per host, and connects with its circuit's `ssh` block.

## How it works

**Reading.** Every refresh runs `iptables -C` with the rule's own arguments, and its exit status says whether the rule is there. A rule deleted by hand shows as out of sync, and the next apply adds it back. iptables answers `-C` the same way for a chain that doesn't exist, so a missing chain reads as a missing rule, and the apply then fails naming the chain. Removing a step whose chain is gone succeeds.

**Applying.** Conn3x adds the rule with `iptables -A`, at the end of the chain, or `iptables -I` with `position = "insert"`: at the top, or at `rule_num`. Where the rule goes only counts when it's added. A rule that's already somewhere in the chain is in sync, wherever it is. Every argument goes to `iptables` as one quoted word, so a `comment` with quotes or a `$` in it arrives as written. `-w` waits for the xtables lock, so the rules of a `for_each` step take turns.

**The rule.** `table`, `chain`, `protocol`, `source`, `destination`, the ports, the interfaces, `ctstate`, `jump` and `comment` are the rule itself, and changing any of them replaces it: the old rule is deleted and the new one added. `destination_ports` becomes `-m multiport --dports`, `ctstate` becomes `-m conntrack --ctstate` and `comment` becomes `-m comment --comment`. Ports need `protocol` to be `tcp`, `udp`, `udplite`, `sctp` or `dccp`. `source` and `destination` are one address or one CIDR network of the step's `ip_version`; a host name or a comma list would make iptables add several rules, which can't be checked as one.

**IPv6.** `ip_version = "ipv6"` uses `ip6tables`. One step is one version, so a rule for both is two steps, or one with `for_each` as above.

**Reboots.** iptables forgets everything at reboot. With `persist = true`, Conn3x saves the whole table after each change with `iptables-save`, to `/etc/iptables/rules.v4` (or `rules.v6`) where Debian and Ubuntu's `iptables-persistent` loads it at boot, or `/etc/sysconfig/iptables` (or `ip6tables`) for the Red Hat family's `iptables-services`, whose `iptables` service must be enabled. The save holds every rule in the table, not only Conn3x's. When neither package is on the host, the step fails and says which to install, rather than write a file nothing reads. A hand edit of the saved file isn't seen: refreshes read the running rules.

**Confirming.** A wrong rule on INPUT is how you lose SSH. With `confirm_after`, the host schedules the command that takes the change back with `systemd-run` before Conn3x makes it, and Conn3x cancels it once a new login works. If that login doesn't come, the host takes the change back by itself, and saves the table again with `persist`. Undoing a removal puts the rule back where it was: Conn3x lists the chain just before the delete, and the undo inserts the rule at that same position, so an `ACCEPT` that sat above a `DROP` goes back above it. `confirm_after` is between `10s` and `1h` and needs systemd on the host.

## Removal

When you delete an `iptables_rule` step, `on_remove` decides what happens on the host. The default is `"delete"`, unlike most modules: Conn3x runs `iptables -D` for the rule, and saves the table with `persist`, so a port you stop managing doesn't stay open. `"forget"` leaves the rule in place.

## From Ansible

`conn3x convert ansible` turns `ansible.builtin.iptables` tasks into `iptables_rule` steps, argument for argument. `action: insert` becomes `position = "insert"`, and `ip_version: both` becomes two steps, one per version. A `match` that only names what another argument already loads, such as `tcp` with `protocol: tcp` or `conntrack` with `ctstate`, is dropped. Ansible's module never saves the rules, so neither does the converted step: add `persist = true` to keep them across reboots.

A task stays for review when it sets `policy`, `flush` or `chain_management`, which change a whole chain; `goto`, `to_ports`, `to_destination` or `to_source`, the NAT and jump options a rule step doesn't carry yet; `limit`; `state: absent`; a `match` with options of its own; a value negated with `!`; or any other argument.
